metadata.working_title: 52-year-old man found behind an auto parts store, brought in to sleep it off
metadata.chief_complaint_patient_voice: I'm just tired. Let me sleep.
metadata.final_diagnosis: Methanol poisoning from drinking windshield washer fluid after his vodka ran out, with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.19, anion gap 30), an osmolar gap of 38 that his ethanol of 28 mg/dL does not explain, and visual impairment from formate. The send-out methanol level, revealed only in the debrief, is 96 mg/dL. He looks like the intoxicated regular the crew says he is.
learning_objectives: When the story says drunk and the respiratory rate and the ethanol level do not fit, get a blood gas and a chemistry and recognize a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
When lactate and ketones do not explain an anion gap, order a measured serum osmolality and calculate the osmolar gap with ethanol in it. A normal osmolar gap does not exclude a toxic alcohol.
Ask an intoxicated patient about his vision. A new visual deficit is a clue to methanol and an indication for dialysis.
Give fomepizole on suspicion without waiting for a methanol level, and know that it stops formate being made and removes none of it.
Give sodium bicarbonate for a pH under 7.30 alongside the antidote. Without it the effect wears off because acid production continues.
Call nephrology for dialysis on the indications (new vision deficit, anion gap above 24, pH 7.15 or lower) without waiting for a level.
metadata.teaching_frame: He is the patient everyone has seen before. The crew knows him, the triage note says he is here to sober up, and he looks it. The only things out of place are a respiratory rate of 27 with clear lungs, an ethanol level too low for how he looks, and eyes he keeps rubbing. The case rewards the learner who chases the number the story does not explain, and then shows that the antidote changes nothing on the monitor.

patient.background:
Long history of heavy drinking. Lives outside, mostly around the same few blocks. Known to the department and to the ambulance crews for intoxication. No other medical history he can give, no medications, no allergies. Smokes. Gets the shakes when he stops drinking, no known withdrawal seizures.

His vodka ran out last night. Some time after that he drank most of a jug of blue windshield washer fluid he found. He cannot say when. The empty jug is in his backpack. He has not eaten for a couple of days. Since waking he has felt sick, with a pounding headache and an aching stomach, and everything has looked blurry and white. Someone saw him sitting slumped behind an auto parts store and called 911. He was not trying to hurt himself.
patient.presenting_appearance: A thin, disheveled man dozing on the stretcher, slurring when roused, unsteady when moved. Breathing fast and deep. Faint smell of alcohol. Cooperative.
patient.arrival_handover: Fifty-two year old man, found sitting behind an auto parts store, slurring and unsteady on his feet. We know him, we bring him in to sleep it off.
patient.handover_authoring_note: Section 2.3. Two sentences, 30 words. No vital sign, no medication, no precipitant. The second sentence departs from the default: it carries history and the crew's framing. That framing is the anchoring the case is built to teach (owner's structure, 11 November 2026). It is never false: he is intoxicated, just not only that.

phase_notes.count_justification: Seven live phases and three terminal. Three untreated tiers on a compressed clock, three held phases because a phase has one set of vitals and fomepizole freezes him at whichever tier he reached, and one improving phase. Bicarbonate without fomepizole and sedation are overlays, not phases.
phase_notes.floor: The untreated_floor phase has no clock. The owner's design constraint is that the patient never arrests, seizes or needs a tube. The narration into it says so openly, and the debrief says what a real patient would do.

prompt.text: Doc, he's breathing awfully fast for someone who's just drunk. Anything you want to check?

case_actions.debrief_note:
A respiratory rate of 27 with clear lungs and a normal saturation is breathing to blow off acid until proven otherwise. His gas showed a pH of 7.19 with a pCO2 of 19 and a bicarbonate of 7: a severe metabolic acidosis with the breathing doing all it can. By Winter's formula the expected pCO2 is 1.5 times 7 plus 8, about 18.5, give or take 2, so this is appropriate compensation and not a second disorder.

Here both gases show the same numbers. In practice venous pCO2 runs a few points higher, and Winter's formula is for arterial pCO2.

A repeat gas is how you see what a treatment did: unchanged after fomepizole alone, better for a few minutes after bicarbonate alone, better and staying better with both. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]

It has to be ordered by name. Measured 328. Calculated: two times the sodium (280) plus glucose over 18 (5) plus BUN over 2.8 (5) is 290. The gap is 38. His ethanol explains 6 to 8 of it. About 30 is unexplained.

The methanol level, a send-out that came back the next day, was 96 mg/dL. Divided by 3.2 that is about 30, the unexplained gap.

The osmolar gap is highest early, while the alcohol is still there, and falls as it is turned into acid and the anion gap rises. A normal osmolar gap late in the course does not exclude a toxic alcohol. correct_disposition.label: Intensive care unit
correct_disposition.explanation:
He goes to intensive care for emergent hemodialysis, a bicarbonate infusion, a gas every few hours and fomepizole every four hours while he is on dialysis.

What the receiving team needs to hear: what he drank and that the level is a send-out, the anion gap and the osmolar gap with the ethanol, his vision, when fomepizole and bicarbonate went in, that nephrology has accepted him, and that the poison center is involved.

alternative_dispositions.label: Step-down or intermediate care with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: He needs emergent dialysis, frequent gases and a bicarbonate infusion in a man whose pH is under 7.2. That is intensive care.

alternative_dispositions.label: General medical ward with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: A ward cannot dialyze him tonight or run the gases this needs.

alternative_dispositions.label: Emergency department observation unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Observation to sleep it off is the plan the triage note offered. His respiratory rate and his ethanol level never supported it.

alternative_dispositions.label: Discharge home
alternative_dispositions.explanation: He has a severe metabolic acidosis and is losing his sight. He came back unresponsive.

alternative_dispositions.label: Transfer to another hospital
alternative_dispositions.explanation: This hospital has dialysis and intensive care. Without them, transfer after fomepizole and bicarbonate would be right.

correct_diagnosis.label: Methanol toxicity
correct_diagnosis.explanation: Washer fluid after the vodka ran out, an anion gap of 30 that lactate and ketones do not explain, an osmolar gap of 38 that his ethanol of 28 does not explain, and snowstorm vision. The send-out methanol level, back the next day, was 96 mg/dL. None of that level was needed to make the diagnosis or start treatment.

additional_diagnoses.label: Anion gap metabolic acidosis
additional_diagnoses.explanation: The mechanism, and the number that makes him a dialysis patient: an anion gap above 24, a pH at or under 7.15 as he drifted, with the breathing doing all it can.

minor_diagnoses.label: Acute alcohol intoxication
minor_diagnoses.explanation: True, and the label that hid everything else. Ethanol 28 mg/dL.

minor_diagnoses.label: Lactic acidosis
minor_diagnoses.explanation: A lactate of 3.6 to 4.6, a small part of a gap of 30.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Ethylene glycol toxicity
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The other toxic alcohol with both gaps, and treated the same way at first: fomepizole, bicarbonate, dialysis. His vision points to methanol and his kidneys are normal. Send both levels.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute alcohol intoxication
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: He is intoxicated, and an ethanol of 28 does not explain how he looks, his breathing, his gap or his eyes. This is the diagnosis that sends him to the hallway.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Alcoholic ketoacidosis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The classic trap: a drinker who has not eaten for days with an anion gap. His beta-hydroxybutyrate is 0.5, so ketones cannot explain a gap of 30, and ketoacidosis does not explain an osmolar gap or his vision.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Lactic acidosis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: His lactate is 3.6. It explains a few points of a gap of 30.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Alcohol withdrawal
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: His tachycardia invites it. He has no tremor, no sweating and no hallucinations, and withdrawal does not cause a gap of 30.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Diabetic ketoacidosis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: His glucose is 90 and his ketones are low.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Optic neuritis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: His optic nerves are injured, by formate, not by inflammation. Name the poisoning that is doing it.

debrief_configuration.key_exams_note: The Physical score reads the tagged exams: the trauma survey (head, neurological, abdominal) is critical (owner, 11 November 2026), and the breathing and lung exams are recommended. This list matches them. Model judgment beyond the owner's decision.
debrief_configuration.intended_path_note: Gas, chemistry, ethanol and osmolality, the drink and the eyes asked about, fomepizole, bicarbonate, the poison center and nephrology, ICU. Bicarbonate before fomepizole reaches improving directly if fomepizole follows while it is still acting.
cross_cutting_teaching_points: A diagnosis has to explain the numbers. 'Just drunk' did not explain a respiratory rate of 27 with clear lungs, or an ethanol of 28 in a man who looked this drunk. When the obvious label leaves a number unexplained, chase the number.

Work both gaps. When lactate and ketones do not explain an anion gap, order a measured osmolality and subtract the calculated one with the ethanol in it. The osmolar gap is highest early and falls as the anion gap rises, so a normal one late does not exclude a toxic alcohol. [UNVERIFIED: Kraut and Mullins, N Engl J Med 2018, not opened]

Ask an intoxicated patient about his eyes. He will not volunteer that everything looks like a snowstorm, and a new vision deficit is both a clue and a dialysis indication. [UNVERIFIED: Roberts et al. 2015 (EXTRIP), read through an abstract page and a summary]

Stop it, buffer it, remove it. Fomepizole stops formate being made and changes nothing you can see. Bicarbonate buffers the acid and wears off if production continues. Dialysis removes it. None of the three waits for a methanol level. [UNVERIFIED: fomepizole prescribing information, read through search]
His breathing was the only thing defending his pH. A sedative, or a ventilator on ordinary settings, takes that defense away.
He never crashed in this case. That was a design choice. Untreated methanol poisoning progresses to coma, seizures and death, and the simulator compresses hours into minutes.
